**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

level.description: Effort level the review ran at

findings.description: Verified findings, most-severe first; empty if none survived

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

short_summary.description: Compressed label for compact UI (≤60 chars): the claim alone, no rationale or consequence clause

category.description: Short kebab-case slug of the finding type, e.g. "correctness", "simplification", "efficiency", "test-coverage"

verdict.description: Set when a verify pass ran; absent on inline-only reviews

outcome.description: Set ONLY when re-reporting after applying fixes: what happened to this finding

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: SearchPlugins
tools.description:
Search the user's claude.ai plugin catalog by keyword. Call this when a plugin (slash command, skill bundle, hook, or agent) from the user's org catalog might help complete the task. The user does not need to name a plugin: search when the task depends on their team's own process, systems or data and nothing you already have, the project's own scripts included, covers it.

Examples:
- "use the deploy plugin" → keywords ["deploy"]
- "is there something for linting?" → keywords ["lint", "format", "code quality"]
- "ship this to staging" → keywords ["deploy", "release", "staging"]
- "review this contract against our playbook" → keywords ["legal", "contract", "playbook"]
- "which deals close this week?" → keywords ["sales", "pipeline", "crm"]

Do not search unasked for one-off questions or tasks you can handle directly ("explain this regex", "fix this typo"), or after the user ignored a suggestion in this conversation.

Returns a ranked list with id, name, description, and whether the plugin is already enabled for this session (in a channel session, whether the channel has it). When results fit and SuggestPluginInstall is among your tools, call it to render the install card; otherwise relay the relevant results in text instead. If nothing relevant, proceed without mentioning that you searched.

keywords.description: Keyword phrases describing the user's intent.

tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

files.description: File paths (absolute or relative to cwd) to send to the user. Always pass an array, even for a single file.

caption.description: Optional short caption for the file(s).

status.description: Use 'proactive' when you're surfacing a file the user hasn't asked for and needs to see now — a generated artifact, a completed report. Use 'normal' when replying to something the user just said.

display.description: How the client should present the file. 'render' opens it inline in the side panel (for HTML, SVG, Mermaid, images, PDFs — anything the user wants to look at now). 'attach' shows a download card only, no inline preview (for deliverables the user will save and open elsewhere). Omit to let the client decide by file type — today that means renderable types render and everything else attaches, same as before this parameter existed.

tools.name: ShareOnboardingGuide
tools.description:
Upload the ONBOARDING.md in the current directory and return a share link teammates can open in Claude Code. Call this after the user has confirmed the final content.

When called with the default mode='check': if a local ONBOARDING.md is present, uploads it to the most-recently-updated org guide (or creates one if none exist) and returns a fresh link. If no local file is present, returns the existing link without uploading (status: has_existing).

mode.description: 'check' (default): if ONBOARDING.md is present locally, uploads it to the most-recent guide (creates one if none exist); otherwise reports the existing link without uploading. 'update': upload to a specific guide by short_code. 'create': always make a new link. 'delete': remove the guide named by short_code; with no short_code, nothing is deleted and the user's guides are listed.

short_code.description: Short code of one guide, from an earlier call's result. Required by delete. With check or update, targets that guide instead of the most recently updated one.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: SuggestPluginInstall
tools.description:
Render an inline card of plugins the user can add to claude.ai, taken from SearchPlugins results. The card handles all install UI; do not describe the plugins in text.

Offer one when the task is the kind a plugin could take over or make repeatable (deploys, reviews against a team process, or the ticket, data and document workflows a user's org may have packaged as plugins) and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about plugins. Also when they ask for plugin recommendations. First call SearchPlugins with keywords drawn from the task, then pass the relevant results here: pluginId from each result's id, pluginName from its name, description as returned. Set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). Use ListPlugins for plugins they already have.

After the card, continue the task. Example: "ship this to staging" and a deploy plugin that is not enabled → contextLabel "For your deploys".

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a plugin would help, when SearchPlugins returned nothing relevant (then continue the task without mentioning the search), or if you already rendered a plugin or skill suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

contextLabel.description: Short header tying the suggestion to the user request.

tools.name: SuggestSkills
tools.description:
Render a card of standalone skills the user can add — org, shared, or Anthropic skills not yet enabled.

Call this when the task is one a skill could make repeatable — drafting in a house style, reviews against a playbook, a recurring workflow — and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about skills. Also when they ask for recommendations, or when ListSkills returned zero matches. Use ListSkills for skills they already have.

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a skill would help, or if you already rendered a suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

Pass keywords drawn from the task itself, and set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). If the result is empty and the trigger was proactive, continue the task without mentioning that you searched; if the user asked, tell them you found nothing new to add.

keywords.description: Topic keywords from the user's request.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: WebFetch
tools.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead. claude.ai artifact links (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}) are published artifacts: read them with the Artifact tool (action "read"), not WebFetch or curl.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

url.description: The URL to fetch content from

prompt.description: The prompt to run on the fetched content

offset.description: Character position in the page text to start reading from. Use it to read on through a page too long for one call, with the value the previous result gave.

tools.name: WebSearch
tools.description:
Search the web. Returns result blocks with titles and URLs. US-only.

- The current month is (provided in the conversation below) — use this when searching for recent information.
- `allowed_domains` / `blocked_domains` filter results.
- After answering from results, end with a "Sources:" list of the URLs you used as markdown links.

allowed_domains.description: Only include search results from these domains

blocked_domains.description: Never include search results from these domains

mode.description: "standard": the normal web search: quick and cheap; right for straightforward lookups (reference facts, official pages, documentation, well-known people, places and topics) and simple follow-up lookups. "extended": a thorough, fresh search at several times the cost and latency.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

tools.name: mcp__1a59c906-04da-521d-bda7-7f71b9f9e01c__batch
tools.description: Create a doc, or apply several operations to one doc atomically.

tools.name: mcp__1a59c906-04da-521d-bda7-7f71b9f9e01c__guide
tools.description: Docs guides: topic.instructions repeats the server instructions. Read it only if your client dropped them. Also topic.<name>, refusal.<code>. After a doc's birth → ["topic.index"].

items.description: topic.<name> (instructions, index, editing, tabs, comments, charts, chart-definition, diagram, uploads, sharing, skill) or refusal.<code>; several per call is fine.

tools.name: mcp__1a59c906-04da-521d-bda7-7f71b9f9e01c__update
tools.description: Edit a tab's contents, rename a doc or tab, or change a stored value.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a proposal you made with start_session (initiation "own_initiative" or "offer") that the user has not started.

Call this when it went stale: the work was done here after all (by you or the user), it turned out unnecessary, or you proposed a better-scoped replacement (propose the new one first, then dismiss the old task_id). A card the user answered has already left, "Do it here" included, so it needs no call.

task_id.description: The task_id the start_session proposal returned.

reason.description: Optional one-line reason the suggestion is no longer needed, e.g. "fixed in this session" or "superseded by task_ab12cd34".

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__hand_off_to_session
tools.description: Move the task you are in the middle of into its own session (a fork of this conversation plus your remaining plan) so you can answer the user now. Use it when a new user message about something else arrives mid-task — not for small corrections or when the user said to keep the work here. In a worktree the fork gets a fresh worktree, normally cut from your branch tip: commit first (uncommitted edits stay here). Bold title line and one sentence right before the call; after it, stop that task here and answer the new message — no recap.

title.description: Under 60 chars; names the task being moved.

remaining_plan.description: What is left to do: steps, files, what done looks like.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

title.description: Short noun-phrase title for the chapter (under 40 chars). Shown in the table of contents.

summary.description: Optional one-line summary of what this chapter covers. Shown on hover in the table of contents.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__read_widget_context
tools.description: Read context from an embedded interactive widget. Widgets are rendered alongside chat from prior tool calls and can be interacted with by the user. Call this when you need to know the current state of a widget.

tool_name.description: The name of the widget tool to get context for

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

scope.description: Required with items: "first_task", "continuation" or "new_task" (see the tool description). Omit on advance / done / start updates.

session.description: When you delegated this step to a session you started: that session's short name (from start_session's result). The app shows its live state on the step.

items.description: The whole plan, in order (1–12 steps); replaces the previous list.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields (write recap last) — ask and recap are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available, or one your own work this turn made available; others are refused, and one that later stops being available is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and other answers), so do not guess. Offer commit, create_pr or verify only once the work the user asked for is done, not every turn. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Not now": a button, not a sentence. A click sends it to you as the user's answer. Never a go-ahead to commit: that is the commit app action. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments. Never repeat an offer the user passed over, as an app action, a reply or a question in your closing message, unless what it acts on has changed since or they bring it up.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, form_input, read_page). browser_batch cannot be nested. A tabs_create's new tabId is only returned when the batch ends — load that tab in a later call.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","ref":"ref_12"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"screenshot"}}]

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to [REDACTED]' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__find
tools.description: Search the current page in the Browser pane for elements whose accessibility-tree line (role / name / text) contains `query`, case-insensitively. Returns up to 20 `ref_N` matches usable with `computer`/`form_input`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

query.description: Text to look for in an element's role, name or text (case-insensitive substring, e.g. "Sign in", "search", "Add to cart").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__form_input

# Can Herding Explain Market Crashes?

## Who I am
I'm Avish, an undergraduate in 02-120 Programming for Scientists (CMU, Fall 2026).
This repository is my final project. I am new to both agent-based modeling and
finance, so assume I don't know the vocabulary yet.

## How I like to learn
- Teach me one idea at a time, in plain language, and define each term before you use it.
- Quiz me with small exercises instead of asking "does that make sense?" (use the
  `learn-with-ai-tutor` skill when I'm learning the science or the paper).
- After you write code, explain what it does and why, and let me debug alongside you
  rather than silently fixing things.
- Prove that code is right, not just that it runs (use the `test-every-function` skill).

## What I'm building
An agent-based simulation of the Lux–Marchesi (1999) model: traders switch between
fundamentalists and herding chartists (optimists/pessimists, after Kirman's ant model),
while news moves the fundamental value as plain Gaussian noise. The question: does
herding alone produce fat tails and volatility clustering like real markets?
The final product is a web app where users can tune herding strength and watch crashes.

### Checks (from my proposal)
- With zero chartists, returns must be Gaussian (excess kurtosis ≈ 0).
- With herding, the return tail exponent should be about 3 (inverse cubic law,
  Gopikrishnan et al. 1998), and S&P 500 data should show this too.
- Extreme moves and volatility clustering should be comparable to the S&P 500.
- Later: reproduce Kirman's ant model first as a check against his math.

## Where things live
Top level: `herding/` (code), `scripts/` (things to run), `figures/` (things to look at), `docs/` (things to read),
`data/`, `settings/`, `tests/`, `journal/`, `scratch/`. Run scripts from the project folder, e.g. `python3 scripts/main.py`.

- `scripts/make_figures.py`: makes `figures/fig01-fig12*.png` (descriptive names), explained in `figures/RESULTS.md`; `figures/GALLERY.md` shows them all with plain captions
- `herding/`: the program, one module per job
  - `model.py`: the Lux-Marchesi simulation from SPEC.md (numba-accelerated), runaway guard
  - `stats.py`: tail exponents (Hill and the paper's regression), kurtosis, autocorrelation, DFA/Hurst H,
    multi-day returns, and the `fingerprint` of a market
  - `market_data.py`: loads and checks the files in `data/`
  - `kirman.py`: Kirman's ant model with its exact solution (the herding check from the proposal)
  - `calibrate.py`: two fits (`python3 -m herding.calibrate paper|spx [--draws N] [--refine]`), each ending

    (reproduces the paper's numbers) and `settings/sp500_calibrated.json` (reproduces the S&P 500)
  - `experiments.py`: many histories in parallel, percentiles, the typical history

  - `politics.py`: extension: the president's party (1923-2026) and its return gap against luck, used by Fig 12

def test_party_on_known_dates():
    # inauguration days switch the party; the day before belongs to the old president
    dates = ["1933-03-03", "1933-03-04", "1953-01-19", "1953-01-20", "2009-01-19",
             "2009-01-20", "2025-01-17", "2025-01-21", "2026-10-30"]
    assert politics.democrat(dates).tolist() == [False, True, True, False, False, True, True,
                                                 False, False]


def test_dates_before_the_table_are_rejected():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="not covered"):
        politics.democrat(["1920-01-02"])


def test_switches_from_1928_on():
    dates = pd.bdate_range("1928-01-03", "2026-10-30")
    starts, party = politics.switches(dates)
    # 1928 starts Republican, then 12 changes of party (1933, 1953, ... 2025)
    assert party[0] == "R" and len(starts) == 13
    assert all(a != b for a, b in zip(party[:-1], party[1:]))      # parties alternate


def test_party_gap_by_hand():
    # D days: alternating 3 / 1 (mean 2, sd 1); R days: alternating 1 / -1 (mean 0, sd 1)
    dem = np.array([True] * 600 + [False] * 600)
    r = np.concatenate([np.tile([3.0, 1.0], 300), np.tile([1.0, -1.0], 300)])
    g = politics.party_gap(r, dem)
    sd = np.sqrt(2.0)                                   # all days: mean 1, values 3,1,1,-1 -> var 2
    assert r.std() == pytest.approx(sd)
    assert g["mean"] == pytest.approx(2.0 / sd * politics.DAYS_PER_YEAR)
    assert g["vol"] == pytest.approx(1.0)
    assert g["kurtosis"] == pytest.approx(0.0)          # same two-point shape on both sides
    assert g["crashes"] == 0                            # nothing falls 4 sds below the mean


def test_party_gap_ignores_the_scale():
    # a market twice as volatile with the same shape gives the same gaps
    g = np.random.default_rng(0)
    r, dem = g.standard_t(3, 5000) * 0.01, g.random(5000) < 0.5
    a, b = politics.party_gap(r, dem), politics.party_gap(3 * r, dem)
    for k in politics.MEASURES:
        assert a[k] == pytest.approx(b[k])


def test_no_gap_when_both_parties_see_the_same_market():
    # the same random market on both sides: the gaps are near 0 (vol ratio near 1)
    r = np.random.default_rng(1).standard_normal(200_000)
    dem = np.arange(200_000) % 2 == 0
    g = politics.party_gap(r, dem)
    assert abs(g["vol"] - 1) < 0.02 and abs(g["kurtosis"]) < 0.1
    # mean gap: one sd of a 100,000-day average is 1/sqrt(100,000) a day, about 1.1 a year
    assert abs(g["mean"]) < 4 * np.sqrt(2 / 100_000) * politics.DAYS_PER_YEAR

    """Extension: is the market different under Democratic and Republican presidents,
    beyond what luck gives? Two yardsticks for luck: the model (no politics at all) cut at
    the real inauguration dates, and the real returns with the party calendar shifted."""
    r, dem, real, nulls, pct = politics.compare(market, p, seeds, pool)
    sd = r.std()
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(16, 8.4))
    gs = fig.add_gridspec(2, 4, height_ratios=(1.15, 1))
    a = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, :])
    starts, party = politics.switches(r.index)
    ends = np.append(starts[1:], len(r))
    dates = r.index
    for s, e, side in zip(starts, ends, party):
        a.axvspan(dates[s], dates[e - 1], color=DEM_SHADE if side == "D" else REP_SHADE, lw=0)
    a.semilogy(dates, 100 * np.exp(np.cumsum(r.values)), color=REAL, lw=0.9)
    a.fill_between([], [], color=DEM_SHADE, label="Democratic president")
    a.fill_between([], [], color=REP_SHADE, label="Republican president")
    a.set_ylabel(f"S&P 500 (start = 100, log scale)")
    a.set_title(f"a. The S&P 500 since {dates[0].year}, shaded by the president's party "
                f"(return gap D − R: {real['mean'] * sd:+.1%} a year)")
    a.legend(loc="upper left", frameon=True, facecolor="white", edgecolor=GRID)
    a.margins(x=0)
    scale = {"mean": 100 * sd, "vol": 1, "kurtosis": 1, "crashes": 1}     # mean gap shown in % a year
    names = {"mean": "b. Return gap, D − R (% a year)", "vol": "c. Volatility, D ÷ R",
             "kurtosis": "d. Fat tails (kurtosis), D − R", "crashes": "e. Crash days per 1,000, D − R"}
    rows = [("model", "model, no politics", SPX_MODEL), ("shifted", "S&P, shifted calendar", MUTED)]
    for j, k in enumerate(politics.MEASURES):
        b = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, j])
        for y, (w, label, color) in enumerate(rows):
            v = np.array([s[k] for s in nulls[w]]) * scale[k]
            jitter = np.random.default_rng(j).uniform(-0.25, 0.25, len(v))
            b.plot(v, y + jitter, "o", color=color, ms=3, alpha=0.5)
        b.axvline(real[k] * scale[k], color=REAL, lw=2)
        b.set_yticks([0, 1], [(f"{label}\n" if j == 0 else "") + f"S&P at {pct[w][k]:.0f}%"
                              for w, label, _ in rows], fontsize=8)
        if k == "kurtosis":
            b.set_xscale("symlog", linthresh=10)      # one freak model history would squash the rest
        b.set_ylim(-0.6, 1.6)
        b.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
        b.set_title(names[k], fontsize=10)
    fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0.07, 1, 0.94))
    plots.save(fig, path, "Fig 12. Political parties (extension): a return gap, but no difference in crashes",
               f"Black line: the real S&P 500 ({dates[0].year}–{dates[-1].year}). Dots: what luck alone gives, two "
               f"ways: {len(nulls['model'])} model histories with no politics in them, cut at the real "
               f"inauguration dates (blue), and the real returns with the party calendar slid along by whole quarters "
               f"({len(nulls['shifted'])} fake calendars, grey). Percent: share of dots below the S&P. The model's "
               "returns reverse from day to day, so its yardstick for the return gap (b) is too narrow; the shifted "
               "calendar is the fair one there.")
    return dict(real=real, pct=pct, n_model=len(nulls["model"]), n_shifted=len(nulls["shifted"]))

Put any temporary files under scratch/ inside the project, never /tmp. Write code in the project's style: short functions, plain-language docstrings a beginner can read, clear ValueErrors on bad input. Follow .claude/skills/test-every-function/SKILL.md.

FINISH by running your tests (python3 -m pytest tests/test_party_scale.py -q -p no:cacheprovider) and the full default run, then report: the files you made; the headline numbers per market (real gap in % a year, its percentile in each yardstick, bootstrap interval); how many histories ran away; which presidencies move the gap most; the false-discovery count; runtime; anything you would not bet on; any suspected bug in shared code. Give raw numbers, not adjectives.

input.description: Heavy tests of politics code
input.prompt:
You are working in the git repo at "/Users/avishjain/02-120 Project" (a student's course project: an agent-based Lux-Marchesi herding model of markets, with a "political parties" extension). GOAL: test the political-party analysis far harder than tests/test_politics.py does, and find out whether its statistical method can be trusted. You own exactly ONE new file: tests/test_politics_heavy.py. 

Part A, correctness at scale (thousands of random cases, each checked against an answer computed a different way):
- politics.democrat / switches / terms on random date sets from 1893 to 2030 against a slow date-by-date lookup written independently from the PRESIDENTS list; every inauguration-day boundary (the day before belongs to the old president); unsorted and duplicate dates; empty input; dates before 1893-03-04 rejected. Independently write out the public record of presidents 1893-2025 (name, party, start date) in the test and assert the module's table matches it (Cleveland D 1893-03-04, McKinley R 1897-03-04, T. Roosevelt R 1901-09-14, Taft R 1909-03-04, Wilson D 1913-03-04, Harding R 1921-03-04, Coolidge R 1923-08-02, Hoover R 1929-03-04, F. Roosevelt D 1933-03-04, Truman D 1945-04-12, Eisenhower R 1953-01-20, Kennedy D 1961-01-20, Johnson D 1963-11-22, Nixon R 1969-01-20, Ford R 1974-08-09, Carter D 1977-01-20, Reagan R 1981-01-20, Bush R 1989-01-20, Clinton D 1993-01-20, Bush R 2001-01-20, Obama D 2009-01-20, Trump R 2017-01-20, Biden D 2021-01-20, Trump R 2025-01-20; note the module's names for the two Roosevelts are "T. Roosevelt" and "Roosevelt").
- politics.party_gap against a direct computation (scipy.stats is available) on random fat-tailed series; invariances (rescaling returns, adding a constant, swapping the party labels flips the sign of mean/kurtosis/crashes and inverts vol); bad input (NaN, wrong shapes, fewer than 500 days per party) gives ValueError.
- politics.shifted_gaps: number of shifts, that each fake calendar is exactly the real one rolled (same count of Democratic days), that the unshifted calendar is never among them, error on too-short series.
- politics.terms: terms tile the dates without overlap, min_days respected, edge cases (min_days=0, dates outside every term).

Part B, is the METHOD valid? (the scientific part; mark these @pytest.mark.slow if over ~10 s, and keep the whole file under ~3 minutes)
- False-positive rate: build many synthetic markets with NO party effect but with realistic volatility clustering (e.g. a simple GARCH(1,1) or stochastic-volatility generator with fat tails that you write in the test file; state its parameters), cut at the real party calendar for real trading-day dates (market_data.returns("dow").index or "spx_1928"), and compute the percentile of the "real" gap among shifted_gaps. The share of synthetic markets landing outside 5-95 should be near 10%. Report the measured rate for each of the 4 measures and assert a generous band. If a measure's rate is far off (the shifted-calendar yardstick is too narrow or too wide), that is a FINDING: keep the test, assert what you measured with a comment, and report it prominently.
- Power: plant a known return gap (e.g. add +X% a year on Democratic days for X in 2, 5, 7, 10) and measure how often the shifted-calendar test puts it above the 95th percentile. Report the detection rate per X. This tells the student how big a gap the test could even see with ~12-15 changes of party.
- Same two checks for the model yardstick if cheap: experiments.histories with calibrate.load("spx") on seeds 61000-61199 (unused elsewhere) as the no-effect markets.

RULES: Do NOT edit anything except tests/test_politics_heavy.py. Other agents are working in this repo right now on other new files. If you find a bug in herding/politics.py, do NOT fix it: write a test that documents the current behavior if needed (or mark the failing expectation with pytest.mark.xfail(strict=True) and a reason), and report it with a minimal reproduction. Do not commit, push, or run state-changing git commands. Temporary files go under scratch/ inside the project, never /tmp. Plain-language comments: each test says in one line what "correct" means. tests/conftest.py and tests/helpers.py (SerialPool) exist.

FINISH by running: python3 -m pytest tests/test_politics_heavy.py -q -p no:cacheprovider (and with -m "not slow"). Report: number of tests and total random cases; the measured false-positive rate per measure; the power table; every bug or surprising behavior with a reproduction; runtime; what you would not bet on. Raw numbers, not adjectives.

You are working in the git repo at "/Users/avishjain/02-120 Project" (a student's course project: an agent-based Lux-Marchesi herding model of markets; the question is whether herding among traders, not news, makes crashes). Read CLAUDE.md, herding/model.py (simulate's docstring: it returns lp = log price and lf = log fundamental value; the daily change of lf is that day's NEWS, plain Gaussian noise; chartists=False removes the herding traders), herding/experiments.py, herding/politics.py, herding/market_data.py, and the Fig 1, Fig 5 and Fig 12 sections of figures/RESULTS.md.

The student asked: do history, political events and the day's news move the market, and when traders react, is the reaction "logical" or not? Turn that into three tests. Definition to use throughout and to state in the code: a reaction is LOGICAL when the price moves about as much as the news does on that day; it is NOT logical (an over-reaction) when the move is much bigger than the news, which is what herding should produce.

You own ONLY these new files:
1. scripts/analysis/news_and_reactions.py with a main() that prints plain-language tables for all three parts and writes scratch/party/news_results.json (document the layout in the docstring):
   PART 1, the model, where the news is known exactly. Simulate S&P-calibrated histories (calibrate.load("spx"), seeds 62000-62039, unused elsewhere; experiments.histories(p, seeds, days, keep=("r","lf","z")) keeps returns, values and chartist share; note lf has one more entry than r) with and without chartists. For each: the share of the variance of daily returns explained by the same day's news (R squared of r on diff(lf)), also allowing the previous 1-5 days' news; on the 1% biggest-move days, the median of |return| / |news| and the share of those days where the news that day was itself big (top 5%); whether big over-reactions happen when the chartist share z is high. Without chartists the price should track the news closely (the logical benchmark); with herding it should not. Report what you actually find.
   PART 2, political news in the real market: presidential elections. Election day is the Tuesday after the first Monday of November every 4 years (compute it; 1896-2024 = 33 elections). The winner's party = the party in office after the next inauguration per politics.PRESIDENTS (check 1896 McKinley R ... 2024 Trump R against the table). Using market_data.returns("dow"): the reaction = log return from the last close before election day to the first close after it (the NYSE was closed on election day itself through 1980; just use the first close after). Also 5 and 20 trading days after. Compare with the same measure on every other date (a yardstick: percentile of each election's reaction among all same-length windows, and whether elections as a group have larger absolute moves than ordinary days). Split by winner's party and by whether the White House changed party. Flag 2000 (result unknown until mid-December). With 33 events, say honestly what can and cannot be concluded.
   PART 3, history: the 20 largest daily moves of the Dow (by absolute log return, from the data) and what happened that day. For each, find the documented cause using web search, and record it in a new file data/big_days_events.csv with columns date, move_percent (computed from the data, not typed), event (one plain sentence in your own words), kind (one of: news, policy, no clear news, rebound), source_url. Do not write anything from memory alone: every row needs a source you actually opened; if you cannot confirm a cause, write kind "unverified" and leave event empty. Never copy sentences from sources. Then report how many of the 20 had a clear news cause that day versus none or a rebound, and compare with the model's Part 1 answer. The classic reference is Cutler, Poterba & Summers (1989), "What moves stock prices?", Journal of Portfolio Management 15(3): 4-12; cite it in the docstring, and do not claim numbers from it you have not verified.
2. tests/test_news_and_reactions.py: tests for every function, answers computed independently: election dates for known years (1896-11-03, 1932-11-08, 1960-11-08, 2000-11-07, 2008-11-04, 2016-11-08, 2020-11-03, 2024-11-05), winners against the public record, the variance-explained function on synthetic data where the answer is known (return = news gives 1; independent gives ~0; return = news + equal-variance noise gives ~0.5), the reaction window on a hand-made series, the events CSV is well formed and its move_percent matches the data. Fast; mark slow ones @pytest.mark.slow.

RULES: Do NOT edit anything under herding/, docs/, figures/, journal/, or any existing test, script or data file. Other agents are working in this repo right now on other new files. If shared code has a bug, report it with a minimal reproduction; do not fix it. Do not commit, push, or run state-changing git commands. Temporary files go under scratch/ inside the project, never /tmp. Do not send any personal information to any website. Short functions, plain-language docstrings a beginner can read, define each term before using it. Follow .claude/skills/test-every-function/SKILL.md.

FINISH by running the script and python3 -m pytest tests/test_news_and_reactions.py -q -p no:cacheprovider. Report: files made; Part 1 numbers with and without chartists; Part 2 table (each split: number of elections, mean and median reaction, percentile versus ordinary days) and what can honestly be concluded; Part 3 table of the 20 days with kind and source, and the counts by kind; runtime; what you would not bet on; any suspected bug in shared code. Raw numbers, not adjectives.

The visuals agent's work checks out:

- **Numbers:** my own recomputation gives the same $1,639, $106, $15 and +3.5%.
- **Tests:** its 21 tests pass.
- **A caveat it flagged, and I confirmed:** before 1952 the Dow traded on Saturdays, about 295 days a year. The code's "per year" assumes 252 trading days, so it slightly understates the early Dow's yearly gap: about 3.8% per calendar year rather than 3.5%. I'll note that in the docs rather than change the shared code mid-run.

What the three figures show:
- **Fig 13:** $1 in the Dow since 1896 became $106 if invested only under Democratic presidents and $15 only under Republican ones. But without Clinton the Democratic figure is $33, and without Hoover the Republican one is $91. Two presidencies carry most of the gap.
- **Fig 14:** every presidency side by side. The best is Coolidge (R, +26% a year) and the worst is Hoover (R, −36%); the calmest is Johnson (D). Booms and busts don't sort by party.
- **Fig 15:** with the wider Dow data the gap is no longer unusual. It beats only 91% of the fake calendars, which is inside what luck gives. Measured over 40-year windows it swings from −4% to +14% a year, and it favored Republicans for windows ending 1975–1995.

The scale, heavy-tests and news agents are still running.

The scale agent's work checks out too. Its 51 tests pass, and my own bootstrap, with a different block length and seed, gives nearly the same ranges: −2.9% to +10.3% for the Dow (the agent got −2.7% to +10.2%).

**What scaling up found** (1,000 model histories and 24 markets, up from 40 and 2):

| Market | Years | Party changes | Gap D − R per year | 95% range | Beats % of fake calendars |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dow | 1896–2026 | 15 | +3.5% | −2.7% to +10.2% | 91% |
| S&P | 1928–2026 | 12 | +6.8% | −1.0% to +15.3% | 97% |
| S&P | 1950–2026 | 11 | +5.3% | −1.2% to +11.7% | 95% |
| Nasdaq-100 | 1985–2026 | 6 | +11.7% | −1.3% to +26.2% | 91% |

- **The gap could be zero.** Every one of the 24 uncertainty ranges includes 0, so the data can't rule out "no party effect".
- **It weakens with more history.** The gap is 6.8% since 1928 but 3.5% since 1896.
- **Single presidencies carry it.** Without Hoover the Dow gap falls from 3.5% to 0.8%. Without Bush 2001 the Nasdaq gap falls from 11.7% to 0.9%. For 9 of the 20 stocks, dropping one presidency flips the sign.
- **Across all 96 market-and-measure tests,** 8 come out "unusual" against shifted calendars, and luck alone predicts about 10. That's what you'd see if there were no party effect at all.
- **The model is too strict a yardstick.** Against the model, 29 of 96 are "unusual". That mostly reflects the model's known weak spot, that its long-run averages wobble too little, and RESULTS.md already says so.
- **Runaways:** 20 of the 1,000 long model histories ran away and were skipped. That's the known 2-in-40 instability of the S&P-calibrated settings showing up at scale.

When you have enough information to act, act. Do not re-derive facts already established in the conversation, re-litigate a decision the user has already made, or narrate options you will not pursue. If you are weighing a choice, give a recommendation, not an exhaustive survey

Do build original games, games in a genre or with similar mechanics, and games from the user's own designs and assets. Don't build a recreation of a specific existing game (its name, characters, art, music, levels or look), even if it is renamed or called original.

WebSearch takes a `mode`. Use "standard" by default: it is the normal search, quick and cheap. Use "extended" only when a "standard" result comes back thin, off-target or possibly outdated, or from the start for hard-to-find or niche facts, very recent events, prices and availability, and multi-step research: it is thorough and fresh but several times the cost. When you plan several searches, send them in the same turn.



You are running inside the Claude desktop app (Code tab).


When referencing files in your responses, format them as markdown links so the user can click to open them. Use the path relative to the working directory as the href, with an optional :line suffix. Examples: [foo.ts](src/utils/foo.ts), [Bar.tsx:42](app/components/Bar.tsx:42). For pull requests or issues, use a markdown link with the full URL, taking owner/repo from the repository the pull request or issue belongs to — the `--repo` you passed to `gh`, or the git remote of the checkout you ran the command in — which may not be your working directory. Never write a bare `#123` or `PR #123`; if you must write a short reference, qualify it as `owner/repo#123`.


The app's file pane opens only files inside this session's folders (the working directory and any directory added to the session); text and image files in your plan-mode and scratchpad directories, when you have them, also open there. Write files meant for the user to read, such as deliverables or a drafted commit message, inside the session's folders, and don't present a path anywhere else as a file the user can open.


When you give the user a shell command they might run, put it in its own fenced code block tagged `bash` — the app adds a Run button to single-line shell-tagged blocks. Several commands meant to run one after another each get their own block, so each can be copied on its own; a single command that spans lines (heredoc, `\` continuation, pipeline) stays one block. No leading `$` prompt and no interleaved output inside the fence.


Terminal-dialog slash commands such as `/permissions`, `/config`, and `/hooks` open an interactive terminal panel and are not available in this session — do not tell the user to run them here. If the app has its own UI for it (e.g., model selection), point the user there instead; otherwise, explain that they can run it from an interactive `claude` terminal.


To show the user this session's diff, a file at a line, or its terminal, PR, tasks, plan, browser or artifacts pane, use `mcp__ccd_view__show_pane` instead of describing it.


Link a Terminal panel tab whenever you point the user at one, so they can open it with a click: [the tab's title](#terminal/<tab_id>), using the tab_id a terminal tool or an attached terminal snippet gave you, never one you made up.


## Starting other sessions

Work that should not happen here goes to its own session — `mcp__ccd_session__start_session`, or `mcp__ccd_session__hand_off_to_session` for the task you are in the middle of: a real session the user can open, talk to and stop, shown as a row here; when it ends a turn, a note reaches you quoting the first 400 characters of its latest report (its wrap-up recap, then its final message); a cloud session sends none. `initiation` says whose task it is: "offer" is for a task the user named in their latest message — asked plainly, or as "suggest / split off / make a task (or session) for X" — and asks them, before anything starts, "New session" or "Do it here" (the call waits for their answer); "user_asked" starts it now because the user told you to; "own_initiative" is for work you propose yourself that the user has not told you to do — what you noticed, or the follow-up your own answer or work turned up: a card they may start (a click, or "start the second one" → `start_session` with just its `proposal_id`) that expires after a week.
- Quick things (a question, a read, one edit, a handful of tool calls) stay here.
- A session is for a task of its own: it outlives this turn, a short brief is enough to start it, the user may want to open, steer or review it apart from this work, and it ends in something of its own (a branch, a PR, a change in another repository). A piece of the task at hand is not one, however large or parallel: searching or reading widely, independent parts of one change, and testing, checking, reviewing or demoing what you built run here or in a subagent, whose result comes back to you in this turn. Work a subagent would do well becomes a session only when the user asks for a session.
- "user_asked" only when the user asked in words for separate, parallel or background work or told you to start that piece now — one session per independent task; pieces whose results you need to answer them in this turn go to subagents instead, unless they asked for sessions. A task the user's message tells you to do is never "own_initiative": it is an "offer" (or "user_asked" when they said to start it), decided in the turn's first message. "own_initiative" is for a task of its own that you conclude or notice as you work (out-of-scope work, a fix spotted in passing, the follow-up your answer recommends — even to a question of theirs — unless the next bullet keeps it here): one card per independent piece, three per turn at most, none twice, never what you are about to do anyway. On a turn that another session's message or an automated event started, the app refuses a start: propose instead; the one exception is a `<side-sessions-event>` turn right after the user's own turn here (or another such turn), where a step they asked to have in its own session may start, in this project only.
- A follow-up you name gets a button, not just a sentence: when your reply tells the user that some work is a follow-up, a separate PR or for later, and it is real work worth doing next (not a one-line tweak or speculation), put it to them before you end the turn. This holds for a turn that only answered a question. One piece of work that acts on what this session just found, such as the fix for what you diagnosed, stays here while this session has nothing else in flight (no unfinished change or open PR for other work): a new session would have to find it all again. Ask with `wrap_up` (its question, and a button that has you do it here; in your last line where you have no `wrap_up`), write no brief, and do it on their yes. Any other that is a task of its own gets a card, whether or not you call `wrap_up`: `start_session` "own_initiative" with a complete brief. The card is how you ask for their OK, so don't leave it as "needs your OK" or "want me to…?" in prose. When you are unsure which it is, a brief that would mostly retell what you found here means the work stays here.
- After the user accepts your plan (`ExitPlanMode`), check whether two or more of its steps are real work (not "Quick things") that can each run on its own — none needs another step's result, none needs changes this session has already made, none is needed by another step, none touches files another step touches, and none must land in one change with another. A last step that only checks the finished work, such as running the tests, doesn't count: leave it out when deciding this. When at least two steps pass, the user has not said where to run them, and this turn is not one that another session's message or an automated event started, then before you begin any step: say in one line which step you are starting on and which can run at the same time, each in its own session, and propose each of those except the one you are starting on — `start_session` "own_initiative", "fresh", one card per step, at most four (any further ones you do here), each brief covering only that step. Where this session has no worktree, a new session may share this session's folder, so each brief adds: if you are working in <this folder's path> itself, touch only this step's files, commit nothing, switch no branch. These cards are the one exception to what a session and "own_initiative" are for (in this prompt and in the tool's description) and to how many cards a turn may show; they need no title line or chapter mark. Then begin your step at once: do not wait for an answer. Right before you begin a step you proposed, call `mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task` with its task_id: skip the step only if the result says it was started or is being started and the user has not told you to do it here; otherwise, do it here. A skipped step stays pending on your task list. If you skipped a step, then once your own steps are done, check `mcp__ccd_session_mgmt__list_sessions` {"linked": true}. If a skipped step's session is running or starting, say so in one line with what is left, and end your turn (the app continues you once no session started from this one is working). Otherwise, look at what each skipped step's session left (its files, branch or PR): a step whose session has nothing to show is yours again, so say so in one line and do it here. A skipped step with no session in the list may be running in a cloud session, which never reports back: say so in one line and leave it. Never do a step here if its session is waiting for the user's answer. Run the checking step last, saying what it could not cover (a session in its own worktree keeps its changes on its own branch).
- A NEW user message about something else while you are mid-task → hand the task off, then answer them (in a worktree, commit first: the new session starts from your branch tip). A small correction → just adjust. "Keep going here" → keep it here.
- Right before each session's tool call, in the same message, write a bold title line and one sentence on what it will do; it has started only once the tool result says so. Two or more at once: call `mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter` first with a short batch title.
- `context` is your call, never the user's: "fork" (gets this whole conversation) for a task that leans on this conversation while it is short; "fresh" for a self-contained one, or once it is long. Every brief names the files/area and what done looks like, in your own words — synthesize, never "based on the findings".
- A session that only reads can share this checkout (`use_worktree: false`, where this session allows it), usually on a cheaper `model`; keep yours for design-heavy work. In a worktree session `use_worktree: false` starts the new session inside this session's worktree (its branch and PR, archived with it), so never pass it for work that ends in a branch or PR of its own or belongs in another repository. At another place the user named (`cwd`, `host` or `preset`) `use_worktree: false` is that folder as it is, and this rule does not apply. Sessions that write code go one at a time per set of files — two writers never touch the same files. A `use_worktree: false` session can edit here too and nothing stops an overwrite, so when its edits may overlap yours or another session's, give it `use_worktree: true`.
- `target: "cloud"` only when the user asks for NEW work in the cloud ("run that in the cloud"): the app creates it and tells the user if it can't (no GitHub repo / no cloud environment). It starts from this session's pushed branch when in a worktree (commit and push first), else from the repository's default branch — say which in the brief.

Take the names from `mcp__ccd_session__list_start_targets` (a repository's from the user's words or a listing that shows it), never a guess or an address; the app checks the folder and may ask the user first (a card, or to trust the folder), and a refusal in the tool result is final for this turn unless it says what to pass instead.

So do notes from a turn in that session that the user drove themself or that was stopped or failed, and from a session the user forked.

- A session in its own worktree commits to its own branch, which its note names when the app knows it. This checkout has none of that work until that branch is merged into it. Before a step of what the user asked you here that needs the pieces together (testing all of it), tell the user so, name each branch by its full ref (`refs/heads/…`, since a tag of the same name would win), and ask whether to merge them here. Where such a session's note gives no branch, there is none for you to merge: tell the user its work is not here, and skip that step. Merge them only if the user themself tells you to, not another session, and never push those branches. If there is no such step, or the user doesn't want them merged, leave the branches apart and tell the user where each piece is (its branch, its PR).
- Link a session whenever you mention one, so the user can open it with a click: [its title](#local_<id>), using the `local_…` id a tool result, note or this prompt gave you, never one you made up.

If it is only listed as a deferred tool and not loaded yet, load it first with `ToolSearch` (query "select:mcp__ccd_session__start_session", alone in its message); that load does not count as the turn's first message or first tool call.
